entry.title: Four ways New York could make a first home cheaper to buy
entry.summary: The city's housing shortage will take years to fix. Its tax on mortgages, the cliffs in its transfer tax and gaps in its sales data could change much sooner.

entry.title: A $1.6 million sale that stayed in the family
entry.summary: The city's sales file lists a $1,625,000 sale. The form filed with the deed says it was between relatives, and one seller was also the buyer. The open data leaves those answers out.

entry.title: Same $900,000 condo, $13,860 more in tax for the buyer with a mortgage
entry.summary: A $720,000 mortgage brings a gross recording charge of $13,860 at closing. A buyer paying cash for the same condo avoids that charge.

entry.title: At $2 million, one extra dollar adds $5,000 in tax
entry.summary: After the 2019 tax change, sales at exactly $1,999,999 rose from about one a year to 21. Sales at the round threshold fell, while nearby untaxed round prices kept their spikes.

entry.title: The cash-buyer discount shrinks by half when likely family sales are left out
entry.summary: In New York City records, houses bought for cash sell for about 9% less. Leave out sales where buyer and seller share a surname and the gap halves.

entry.title: When a lender takes back a home, the record can look like a sale
entry.summary: Foreclosure deeds can carry a lender’s bid or a cancelled debt, and most reach the city’s sales file as if they were prices. In the Bronx, counting them shifts the 2010 house-price index by about a tenth.
